_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III: the Farud episode, the snowstorm, Piran's night-attack. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.en: Farud Beholds the Army of Iran

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Farud secs. 11-12

summary.en: Farud, the unrecognized son of Siyawush, hears that a host marcheth from Iran against Turan for vengeance. Jarira counsels him: thy brother is the new Shah of Iran; thou shouldst be foremost in the race for vengeance — go with Tukhar and look for the blazons of Bahram and Zanga, for he and these twain were never separable. From the summit of a lofty mountain the two view the Iranian host defiling between two mountains: what with golden helm and golden shield thou wouldst have said no gold is left unmined, a cloud hath risen and rained jewelry.
summary.zh: 西亞瓦什不為人知的兒子法魯德聽聞伊朗大軍為復仇而來。母親賈里拉勸道：「你的兄長正是伊朗新王；你當率先復仇！」並囑他隨圖卡爾上山，尋找巴赫拉姆與贊加的旗徽——他們與其父形影不離。二人立於高山之巔俯瞰：金盔金盾、金斧金戈，彷彿「天下之金已盡採，雲中降下寶石之雨」。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Farud is killed by his brother's army through Tus' haste — a tragedy of mistaken kinship. No living community restriction.

passages.text: News reached Farud: the bright sun's face is darkened by dust raised by the feet of elephants and camels; a host marcheth from Iran against Turan for vengeance, purposing to take the road that leadeth to Kalat. The inexperienced youth on hearing this grew very sore of heart and dark of soul. He came down from the hold, unbarred the gate, and going forth surveyed the lofty mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Jarira said to him: thy brother is the new Shah of Iran; a world-lord shrewd is Kai Khusrau, and he well knoweth both thy name and native worth. One father's blood and bone are in you both, and Siyawush was peerless in the world. Now, since thy brother seeketh to avenge the soul of Siyawush, thou shouldst be foremost in the race for vengeance. In the dust afar raised by the host look for two cavaliers, Bahram and Zanga son of Shawaran; he and these twain were never separable, they were his lords, he was their over-lord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 11 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They chose the summit of a lofty mountain, commanding all the army of Iran, and marvelled at the troops and their equipment. The Iranian host defiled between two mountains, and what with golden helm and golden shield, with golden ax and golden partisan, thou wouldst have said: no gold is left unmined, a cloud hath risen and rained jewelry! The roar of kettledrums along the pass affrayed the vultures as they flew o'erhead, while thirty thousand sword and buckler men marched bravely on in all points dight for war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 12 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Death of Farud and of Jarira
title.zh: 法魯德之死與賈里拉自刎

region.zh: 薩帕德山堡（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Farud secs. 20-21

summary.en: Jarira dreams that from the lofty castle a flame rose in front of Farud, burning all the castle and the women-slaves, and wakes to see the mountain filled with mail and spears. Farud fights alone till Ruhham strikes his shoulder and Bizhan houghs his steed; dying, he bids the slaves fling themselves from the battlements that none may be the portion of Bizhan, and the beloved Farud plucked out their lives. Jarira kindles a pyre, burns the treasures, hamstrings the steeds, presses her cheeks upon his face, rips up herself and dies upon his breast, and Tus, with beard like camphor, sheds a stream of tears of blood.
summary.zh: 賈里拉夢見城堡起火焚盡侍女，驚醒見滿山甲兵。法魯德孤身力戰，被魯哈姆斫傷肩臂、比讚砍斷馬足；彌留之際他命侍女跳下城牆「免遭比讚之辱」，隨即嚥氣。賈里拉點火焚財、刺廢戰馬，將面頰貼上兒子的臉，自刎於其胸。圖斯鬚如樟腦，泣血如注。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the tragedy of Farud is a canonical Shahnama lament. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Now when the shining sun had disappeared, and dark night led its host across the sky, the daughter of Piran approached her son Farud with anxious mind and aching heart. She dreamed that from the lofty castle rose a flame in front of him she loved so well, illuming Mount Sapad and burning all the castle and the women-slaves. She woke in pain and went out upon the wall, and looking round saw all the mountain filled with mail and spears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Farud descended from the castle-ramparts with all his gallant Turkmans, but of the Turkmans no cavalier remained with him; he fought alone. Ruhham sought with Bizhan to intercept him: Bizhan was staggered by the young man's stroke and lost both sense and power; Ruhham behind struck the lion-man upon the shoulder, and his hand fell useless. Wounded he cried out, and Bizhan came up and houghed his steed as he neared the hold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is no marvel that ye pluck your hair, said dying Farud; the Iranians will come with girded loins to sack the hold and make my slave-girls captive. Let all whose hearts and cheeks burn for my life go fling themselves down from the battlements that none may be the portion of Bizhan. His mother and the female slaves plucked out the scented tresses of their musky hair, while the beloved Farud plucked out their lives: the throne was strewn with hair, the house all sorrow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now when in failure thus had passed away Farud, the hapless son of Siyawush, the slave-girls scaled the roof and dashed them to the ground. Jarira kindled a pyre and burned the treasures; sword in hand she locked the stable of the Arab steeds, hamstrung, and ripped them up. All blood and sweat she sought the couch of glorious Farud, and, having pressed her cheeks upon his face, ripped up herself and died upon his breast. They built upon the mountain-top a royal charnel wherein they placed a throne of gold, and set him there; beside the prince they set Rivniz and great Zarasp, while Tus, with beard like camphor, shed a stream of tears of blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 21 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: The Snowstorm on the Kasa Rud

region.zh: 卡薩魯德河（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Farud secs. 23-24

summary.en: On the Iranian side a tempest rose: a dense cloud came like flying dust, their lips congealed with cold, the tents and camp-enclosures were turned to ice, snow carpeted the mountains, and for a sennight's space earth disappeared. They slew and ate their horses; multitudes of men and cattle perished, and none at last possessed a charger. To pass the barricade of faggots on the river, old Giv girds up his loins — I can burn a flinty mountain with my breath — kindles the pile with a javelin-point, and after three weeks of conflagration, wind, and smoke the army went across the river, for the fire was spent.
summary.zh: 伊朗軍營驟起風暴：黑雲挾塵、唇凝於寒、帳幕成冰、積雪封山，七日之間大地無蹤。士卒宰馬而食，人畜死傷無數，最後竟無一馬可騎。為通過河上柴薪障壘，老將吉夫束腰請命：「我一口氣能燒穿燧石之山！」以鏢尖引火焚壘；烈焰、狂風與濃煙封路三週，第四週柴盡火熄，大軍方渡。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: A tempest rose and none took thought of fight; a dense cloud came like flying dust, their lips congealed with cold, the tents and camp-enclosures were turned to ice, snow carpeted the mountains, and for a sennight's space earth disappeared. There was but little food or rest or sleep: thou wouldst have said earth's face is turned to stone. They slew and ate their horses; multitudes of men and cattle perished. When the eighth day came the sun prevailed, the earth was like a sea, the troops were mustered, and Tus spake of fight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Giv said: this will not be a toil, or, if it be, a toil not unrequited. Bizhan was grieved: I cannot give consent to this; thou rearedst me in stress and hardihood; it must not be that I a youth sit still while thou an old man girdest up thy loins. Giv said: my son, I took this enterprise upon my shoulders; 'tis the time for arms, not for indulgence and decrepitude; be not in dudgeon at my going, I can burn a flinty mountain with my breath.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He passed the Kasa rud albeit with stress, the world for warp and woof had ice and snow, and when he reached the barricade of faggots its length and breadth were more than he could tell; he used a javelin-point to kindle fire, threw it upon the mass and burned the pile. For three weeks conflagration, wind, and smoke allowed no passage through the burning mass, but when the fourth week came the army went across the river, for the fire was spent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 23 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Piran's Night-Attack on the Drunken Host

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Farud sec. 27

summary.en: Out of that noble host Piran made choice of thirty thousand horse who marched at dead of night; no tymbal sounded, no trumpet blared, none raised the battle-cry. The Turkmans marched upon the Iranian host, all drunken and disposed in groups unarmed, and Giv, that fight-engrosser, was astound. Arraying his body in the mail of Siyawush, raging like a leopard at himself in shame for his own indolence, Up! Up! the enemy hath come while we, the warriors of the Shah, are sleeping! The flags were rent, the kettledrums over-turned, for sires had lost their sons and sons their sires, and that great host was utterly overthrown.
summary.zh: 皮蘭自大軍中精選三萬騎，深夜潛行——無鼓、無號、無喊殺。突厥人撲向沉醉的伊朗軍營；吉夫驚醒，披上西亞瓦什的鎧甲，羞憤自斥：「起來！起來！敵人來了，王的戰士還在酣睡！」旗裂鼓翻，父失其子、子失其父，大軍潰不成軍。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Out of that noble host Piran made choice of thirty thousand horse with scimitars, who marched at dead of night; no tymbal sounded, no trumpet blared, none raised the battle-cry. Thence like a murky cloud the Turkmans marched upon the Iranian host, all drunken and disposed in groups unarmed; howbeit Giv was in his tent alert, Gudarz the chieftain sober. Then arose the war-cry with the crash of battle-axes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 27 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gallant hero lion-like arrayed his body in the mail of Siyawush, and, raging like a leopard at himself in shame for his own indolence and sloth: Up! Up! How is it that to-night my brain is filled with fumes instead of war? The enemy hath come while we, the warriors of the Shah, are sleeping! The Iranians were hemmed in; soft pillows were beneath the drunkards' heads, above were sword, hot mace, and scimitar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 27 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now when dawn showed forth from the Sign of Leo, and gallant Giv surveyed the host, he saw the waste all covered with Iranian slain. The flags were rent, the kettledrums over-turned, and the survivors' cheeks like ebony, for sires had lost their sons and sons their sires, and that great host was utterly overthrown. Unable to resist they turned their backs, abandoning their camp in their confusion, and on this wise fared they toward the Kasa rud, a strengthless mob.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Farud sec. 27 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
